enjoyment.title: A little progress you can see
enjoyment.copy: Each fitted piece gives immediate feedback. A scattered image becomes a finished scene; the appeal can be the process as much as the result.
enjoyment.evidenceType: Editorial interpretation of task characteristics; not a measured population-wide preference.

enjoyment.title: An image worth spending time with
enjoyment.copy: Looking for color, texture and shape gives attention a specific job. Sorting, rotating and matching pieces recruits several visual and spatial abilities.
enjoyment.evidenceType: Study-supported cognitive demands; not a promise of cognitive improvement.

enjoyment.title: A pause, a shared table, a personal pace
enjoyment.copy: Try a screen-free ritual, an easy conversation around a table, or a quiet solo project. Choose the difficulty for the experience you want and stop whenever you like.
enjoyment.evidenceType: Suggested experiences, not medical or prevalence claims.

enjoyment.title: What the research actually says
enjoyment.copy: A 2018 trial randomized 100 healthy adults aged 50+ to 30 days of puzzling plus counseling or counseling alone. Puzzlers improved puzzle skill, but not overall visuospatial cognition compared with the control group. Lifetime experience correlations do not establish causation. Ravensburger funded the study and supplied puzzles.

history.title: Education before entertainment
history.copy: London engraver and map seller John Spilsbury is widely credited with early jigsaw puzzles. The National Portrait Gallery dates his puzzle to 1766. These origins connect naturally to map-based teaching; avoid presenting the identity of the first inventor as settled.

history.title: A format with many branches
history.copy: Modern publishers offer standard rectangles, panoramic, shaped, double-sided, wooden and specialty finishes. A piece count is one design choice among image complexity, cut style, piece size and finished dimensions.

formats.label: Small counts
formats.guidance: A manageable first project or a shorter ritual. Dense art or tiny pieces can still make a small puzzle challenging.

formats.label: Everyday adult puzzle
formats.guidance: A practical first physical prototype for original illustration. Inspect finished dimensions and actual piece size.

formats.label: An extended project
formats.guidance: More sorting and more table space. Complexity also depends on repeated colors, detail, cut and reference image. Avoid guaranteed completion times.

formats.label: Larger pieces
formats.guidance: Larger pieces and strong image contrast can make handling and visual matching more comfortable. Counts alone do not establish accessibility.

formats.label: Change the format
formats.guidance: Try round, shaped, panoramic, double-sided or wooden puzzles. Repeated patterns and irregular outlines create different challenges. Foil or gloss can introduce glare.

physicalRecommendations: Offer a 100–300-piece or large-piece option as well as the main 500/1000-piece version.
Use distinct color-and-texture zones, clear objects, readable reference art and a matte proof to assess glare.
List finished width/height, actual piece size if known, cut style and required table space.
Offer sorting trays, comfortable lighting, a movable board and permission to take breaks.
Test with people who have different visual, dexterity and sensory preferences; do not call an untested design universally accessible.
digitalRecommendations: Every piece should have a keyboard-operable placement alternative with an accessible name and visible focus.
Provide row/column destinations, undo/reset and a full reference image.
Use an optional timer only; no compulsory racing, flashing feedback or music playback.
Honor reduced motion and do not use color alone to communicate placement or progress.
accessibility.status: Design recommendations; not validated accessibility claims.

workflow.action: Choose the audience, target age, count, finished dimensions, difficulty, cut style and target retail price. Keep the initial pilot to one or two concepts.
Create or commission original art; document the artist agreement and all source licenses. Keep brands, celebrity likenesses, album covers and protected characters out unless separately licensed.

Use the selected supplier’s exact puzzle and box templates. Keep essential details within safe areas; extend artwork through bleed; proof RGB-to-print color conversion rather than assuming a screen match.
Cardboard products may print onto chipboard or laminated paper surfaces; POD methods vary. Confirm board thickness, paper, adhesive, print method, finish and expected durability for the exact SKU.
workflow.type: Project recommendation informed by supplier examples

workflow.action: Compare ribbon/grid and random cuts. Conventional cardboard puzzles use die cutting; wooden examples can use laser cutting. Confirm false-fit risk, edge quality, cut registration and replacement-piece feasibility.
workflow.type: Project recommendation informed by supplier examples

workflow.action: Inspect a physical production sample at final size: color, detail, glare, piece fit, dust, completeness, edge durability, odor and box damage. Have multiple people build it and record confusion and enjoyment.

Specify inner bag, durable right-sized box, reference insert, artist credit, count, completed dimensions, age grading, required warnings, product/batch identification and support instructions. Include inbound freight and outer shipping protection in cost.
Approve the sample, rights, exact SKU testing, landed quote and fulfillment plan before offering a physical product for sale. These PointCast concepts are development proposals.

printNotes.copy: The verified 19-inch square CJP SKU specifies at least 150 DPI, RGB or CMYK inputs and 3–6 mm bleed. These are that SKU’s instructions, not universal print rules.

Printful’s general puzzle page recommends PNG/JPEG at 300 DPI. For a 20 × 15-inch target at 300 DPI, the art area alone is 6000 × 4500 pixels, before supplier bleed. This is a calculation, not a supplier requirement for every product.
Web concept images do not automatically meet production resolution. Resampling does not restore missing detail; approve an intended-size physical proof before describing art as print ready.

wasteNotes: Right-size packaging and compare freight volume, material weight, damage rate and replacement rate.
Ask for traceable board/material documentation and certification scope for the specific SKU. A website statement does not certify a new PointCast product.
Evaluate coatings, mixed materials, inner bags, adhesives, inks and local disposal instructions together; avoid blanket recyclable, biodegradable, sustainable or eco-friendly claims.
Use small pilots to reduce unsold inventory and track material loss from setup, cutting, damaged stock and returns.

rights.copy: Use original human-created work, licensed work with merchandise rights, or verified public-domain material. An artist agreement should cover puzzle manufacture, packaging, online display, territory, duration, editions, attribution, compensation and approval. Preserve source records; purchasing a print or finding an image online does not itself grant merchandise rights.
rights.aiCopy: US Copyright Office guidance says AI output can qualify only where human authorship determines sufficient expressive elements; prompts alone are insufficient. Record tool provenance and human editing. Describe original generated concept art honestly without promising exclusive copyright or clearance of every possible claim.

safety.market: United States research; reassess each destination market before sale.
safety.copy: Decide the actual intended age and materials before selecting tests or labels. CPSC says ASTM F963 covers toys intended for under-14s; third-party testing and Children’s Product Certificates generally apply to toys intended primarily for children 12 or younger. Its current page identifies ASTM F963-23 for toys manufactured after 2024-04-20. Identify applicable sections for the exact SKU rather than relying on a generic supplier badge.
safety.smallPartsCopy: CPSC’s small-parts ban concerns relevant products intended for children under three, with stated material/product exceptions. Certain children’s toys with small parts require warnings, including in advertising. Do not make a blanket legal classification for all cardboard, wooden or adult puzzles. An adult label alone is not a substitute for appropriate design and marketing assessment.
testChecklist: Confirm market and age classification with the manufacturing/testing specialist.
Ask for exact SKU/batch evidence for applicable material, coating, chemical, edge and mechanical requirements.
Check completeness, cut/fit, damage in transit and repeated-use performance.
Keep test reports, material declarations, manufacturer/importer identification and traceability records.
safety.status: Educational planning guidance; no PointCast puzzle is certified or approved.

business.status: Illustrative classroom assumptions, not forecasts or supplier quotes. No PointCast physical product is offered for sale.
business.formula: Unit contribution = merchandise revenue + shipping collected − product/box/inbound landed cost − shipping paid − pick/pack − payment/channel fees − returns/damage allowance − other variable costs. Break-even units = ceil(fixed launch costs / positive unit contribution). If contribution is zero or negative, there is no profitable unit-volume break-even.

models.name: Small physical pilot
models.assumptions: 50–99 units, one or two concepts; CJP table $18.20 per unscoped default-bag set is only a benchmark. Add box, reference, inbound freight, testing and defects.
questions: Does the sample feel good to build?
Will buyers pay enough after shipping?

models.name: Direct retail edition
models.assumptions: Illustrative merchandise price USD 32–40; landed product USD 12–22; handling USD 1.50–3; seller-paid postage USD 7–10; return/damage reserve 2–5% of merchandise revenue. These ranges are teaching assumptions, not quoted production costs.
questions: Which cost is included in the quote?
Does customer-paid shipping change conversion and contribution?

models.name: Retailers and wholesale
models.assumptions: Test an assumed wholesale price of 50% of a USD 36–40 retail price, then model actual case size, carton freight, payment terms, returns and sales commissions. 50% is a scenario, not a verified universal industry rule.
questions: Is contribution positive at the wholesale price?
How much cash is tied up before payment?

models.name: License the collection
models.assumptions: A manufacturing/publishing partner could pay a negotiated advance or royalty. A 4–8% royalty can be used as a classroom sensitivity example only; no market norm or partner commitment is claimed.
questions: Who approves proofs and controls credits?
Who owns inventory, testing and product liability?

models.name: An optional puzzle series
models.assumptions: Test a quarterly series before a monthly model. Include new-art cadence, cohort retention, pauses/cancellations, reserve stock, repeat postage and acquisition cost; do not model every subscriber as permanent.
questions: Will subscribers want the next edition?
What happens if an edition is late?
Can people choose difficulty or opt out?

workedSensitivity.status: Illustrative only; all costs except the cited card-fee formula are assumptions.

scenarios.name: Merchandise price falls to USD 32; fee and 3% reserve adjusted

workedSensitivity.excluded: Owner pay, acquisition ads, storage, insurance, taxes, unsold units and any additional fixed operating cost. Include them before a real investment decision.

operatingRecommendations: Record supplier quotes with SKU, count, dimensions, board, finish, box, bag, insert, tooling, freight, duty/tax, sample, testing, defect allowance and lead time separately.
Model customer-paid and subsidized shipping, domestic and international delivery separately.
Budget a missing/damaged-piece resolution path; supplier return limits can be narrower than a retailer’s customer promise.
Track sell-through, cash conversion, unsold inventory, waste, refund rate, acquisition cost and reorder demand.
Classroom tasks for the UES Business Concentration: customer interviews, channel margin sheet, break-even sensitivity and pilot decision memo.
Classroom tasks for Design School: image legibility, crop/bleed, cut interaction, packaging prototype and inclusive user test.
IndustryNext case-study angle: compare POD, bulk die-cut board, wooden laser cuts and art licensing using actual evidence; label it proposed study, not a partnership.
